qs.q: Take a (focused) history.
a: Pain (SOCRATES): flank (upper ureter) → radiating to groin/testis (distal stone near the VUJ); sudden, colicky, intermittent; severity; aggravating/relieving.

Urinary symptoms: storage (frequency, urgency, nocturia), voiding (weak stream, hesitancy, straining, incomplete emptying, dribbling), dysuria, haematuria (colour, clots, timing: initial = urethra, terminal = bladder neck/prostate, total = anywhere).
N/V, fever (changes the whole plan), constitutional symptoms.

Risk factors: low water intake, high-protein/salt diet, previous stones (how managed), gout, UTI, family history; drugs (anticoagulants, rifampicin, allopurinol); beetroot; trauma/instrumentation; PMH (DM, HTN), smoking.
qs.why: Renal colic is diagnosed from the pain pattern (sudden, colicky, loin to groin); radiation tells the stone's level; urinary symptoms, haematuria and fever separate stone, infection and obstruction.
hist: Pain moves with the stone: flank for upper ureter, groin/testis as it approaches the VUJ.
Ureteric peristalsis against the stone causes waves of severe colic.
Patients with colic move around; peritonitis keeps patients still.
A stone near the VUJ irritates the bladder.
Exclude outflow obstruction (BPH) as a differential or contributing cause.
Timing localises the source — initial = urethra, terminal = bladder neck/prostate, total = anywhere above.
An infected obstructed kidney is an emergency — needs urgent drainage (stent or nephrostomy), not just pain relief.
Concentrated urine and dietary factors promote stones.
Recurrence is common and guides treatment.
Uric acid stones; struvite stones with infection; inherited metabolic disorders.
Anticoagulants and rifampicin cause haematuria or red urine; beetroot causes red urine (pseudo-haematuria).
Comorbidities; smoking is a risk factor for urothelial cancer causing haematuria.

qs.q: What is the (most likely) diagnosis?
a: Renal/ureteric stone (renal colic); ARC3: right renal stone.
qs.why: Sudden severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with haematuria = urinary stone.

qs.q: What investigations will you order?
a: Urine: dipstick, urinalysis (RBC, WBC, nitrites, pH, crystals), culture & sensitivity (especially with fever).
Blood: CBC, renal profile (creatinine most important), electrolytes, Ca, uric acid (± PTH).
Imaging: non-contrast CT KUB (gold standard).
qs.why: Urine shows haematuria and infection; creatinine tells whether obstruction is harming the kidney; calcium/uric acid look for a metabolic cause; non-contrast CT is the gold standard.

qs.q: What is the type/modality of this image (and the cut)?
a: Non-contrast CT abdomen & pelvis — axial or coronal cut (or IVP for ARC5).
qs.why: No contrast is used for stones (contrast would hide them); state the cut — axial or coronal.

qs.q: What are the findings on the provided imaging?
a: e.g. Left renal pelvis stone + left hydronephrosis (430A/435); left staghorn calculus + hydronephrosis (ARC2); right renal pelvis stone (ARC3/ARC4); left proximal ureteric stone + left hydroureteronephrosis (ureteric-stone stations); left ureteric stone on IVP (ARC5).
qs.why: Always state the side, the site (renal pelvis, ureter, staghorn) and the consequence (hydronephrosis/hydroureter).

qs.q: Where is the stone located?
a: Proximal (upper) ureter — above the pelvic brim/line (SI joint).
qs.why: Ureteric thirds are defined by the sacroiliac joint/pelvic brim — the level guides treatment (URS vs ESWL).

qs.q: Mention other imaging modalities.
a: US, plain KUB X-ray, MRI (IVP).
qs.why: US (no radiation — pregnancy, children), plain KUB (radio-opaque stone follow-up) and MRI/IVP are alternatives to CT.

qs.q: Mention other symptoms the patient may present with. (2)
a: Nausea & vomiting, haematuria, frequency/urgency/dysuria, symptoms of uraemia.
qs.why: Renal colic is often accompanied by vomiting (shared splanchnic innervation), haematuria and irritative bladder symptoms from a distal stone.

qs.q: What is the ER / first-line management?
a: Analgesia (IM/IV diclofenac — NSAID), hydration, antiemetics, ± antibiotics; medical expulsive therapy with an α-blocker (tamsulosin) for distal stones.
Call the urologist!! (they really wanted this answer).
Obstructed + infected → urgent urinary drainage (JJ stent or nephrostomy).
qs.why: NSAIDs are the best analgesics for colic (reduce ureteric spasm and oedema); α-blockers help distal stones pass; an infected obstructed kidney must be drained urgently. Examiners want you to involve urology.

qs.q: Mention treatment modalities / the best intervention. (least → most invasive)
a: ESWL (non-invasive) → ureteroscopy (laser) → PCNL (percutaneous nephrolithotomy) → open surgery (rarely).
Renal pelvis stone: ESWL or PCNL (ureteroscopy is not correct here). Staghorn: PCNL. Ureteric stone: URS (or ESWL); 441A answered PCNL/ureteroscope.
qs.why: The intervention depends on stone size and site — ESWL for small renal stones, URS for ureteric stones, PCNL for large (> 2 cm) and staghorn stones.

qs.q: What complication may he develop? / He returns with fever, chills and flank pain — diagnosis and management?
a: Obstructive pyelonephritis → admit, urine & blood cultures, IV antibiotics, urgent decompression (JJ stent or nephrostomy tube).
qs.why: Fever with an obstructing stone = infection behind obstruction (pus under pressure) — urosepsis risk; antibiotics can't reach it, so urgent drainage is needed.

qs.q: What are the indications for admission?
a: Intractable pain, intractable N/V, fever/pyelonephritis (infected obstructed kidney), renal impairment, solitary kidney, failure of medical therapy.
qs.why: Admit when the kidney or patient is at risk: infection, renal impairment or solitary kidney, or symptoms not controlled orally.

tips.t: 436F: "Ask EVERYTHING — fever, chills, rigors, nausea, vomiting, detailed flank pain, LUTS, previous stones and how they were managed."
Points are deducted if you don't mention the side.

qs.q: What is this?
a: Foley (indwelling urethral) catheter.
qs.why: A two-way catheter with a balloon port = Foley (indwelling) catheter.

qs.q: Name 3 indications.
a: Acute urinary retention (e.g. enlarged prostate); accurate urine-output monitoring (shock, surgery, critically ill); anaesthetised/sedated or comatose patients; incontinence;
immobility/paralysis; after urethral/bladder surgery.
qs.why: Catheters relieve retention, measure urine output accurately, and manage patients who can't void.

qs.q: Name 4 complications.
a: UTI (especially long-term), urethral trauma/false passage/stricture, epididymitis, haematuria, bladder stones (bladder cancer long-term), paraphimosis.
qs.why: The foreign body allows bacteria to ascend (UTI), can injure the urethra (stricture, false passage), and causes stones/irritation in the long term; a retracted foreskin left behind causes paraphimosis.

a: Absolute: urethral trauma, urethral stricture; relative: infection → use a suprapubic catheter.
Types: indwelling (Foley), straight (in-out), condom catheter. Size in French (Fr).

title: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction (antenatal hydronephrosis)
scenario: An 18-month-old with prenatal hydronephrosis on US; US repeated post-natally (left and right kidneys shown). (new case) 442A · 442B

imgs.cap: US left kidney — marked pelvicalyceal dilatation US right kidney — normal
442B version — left kidney, dilated pelvis (measured) 442B version — right kidney

qs.q: What do you see?
a: Left hydronephrosis (normal right kidney).
qs.why: Compare both kidneys: a dilated pelvicalyceal system on one side only = unilateral hydronephrosis (state the side).

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Pelvi-ureteric (ureteropelvic) junction obstruction.
qs.why: Unilateral hydronephrosis without a dilated ureter in a child = PUJ obstruction, the commonest cause.

qs.q: How would you manage it initially?
a: IV fluids/hydration, prophylactic antibiotics; (MAG3 renogram to assess function & drainage, follow-up US).
qs.why: Most are observed: antibiotic prophylaxis prevents UTI while a MAG3 renogram assesses drainage and split function, with serial US.

qs.q: What are the indications for surgery?
a: Worsening hydronephrosis, reduced split renal function, bilateral disease, poor family compliance, poor hospital set-up (also recurrent UTIs, pain, stones).
qs.why: Surgery is indicated when the kidney is being harmed (falling function, worsening dilatation) or symptoms/infections occur.

qs.q: What is the name of the surgery?
a: Pyeloplasty (Anderson–Hynes dismembered).
qs.why: Anderson–Hynes pyeloplasty excises the narrowed PUJ and re-anastomoses the ureter to the pelvis.

imgs.cap: CT urogram — filling defect in the bladder (arrow)

qs.q: What is this test?
a: CT urogram.
qs.why: Contrast outlining the collecting systems and bladder in the excretory phase = CT urogram.

qs.q: What is this finding called?
a: A filling defect of the urinary bladder.
qs.why: A tumour projecting into the contrast-filled bladder shows as a filling defect.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Transitional cell (urothelial) carcinoma of the bladder.
qs.why: A bladder filling defect in a smoker with haematuria = urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma.

qs.q: What is the commonest presentation?
a: Painless (total) haematuria.
qs.why: Bladder cancer classically presents with painless visible haematuria.

qs.q: What is the most common risk factor?
a: Smoking.
qs.why: Smoking causes about half of bladder cancers (carcinogens excreted in the urine).

title: Urethral injury (pelvic fracture)
scenario: After a road-traffic accident, ABCD done, pelvic fracture stabilised; the team failed to insert a Foley catheter (written station). 430F · Archive

imgs.cap: Retrograde urethrogram — extravasation of contrast with pelvic fracture

qs.q: What is the type of injury?
a: Posterior (membranous/prostatic) urethral injury.
qs.why: Pelvic fractures shear the membranous urethra at the urogenital diaphragm — a posterior urethral injury.

qs.q: Mention 4 signs you can find.
a: Blood at the meatus (without voiding), high-riding prostate on PR, distended bladder / inability to void, perineal ecchymosis/butterfly haematoma, inability to pass a catheter.
qs.why: Blood at the meatus, a high-riding prostate, perineal bruising and retention are the signs that forbid blind catheterisation.

qs.q: What is the imaging modality in the picture?
a: Retrograde urethrogram (RUG).
qs.why: Contrast injected retrogradely from the meatus = retrograde urethrogram, the test for urethral injury.

qs.q: What do you see in the picture?
a: Extravasation of contrast (and pelvic fracture).
qs.why: Contrast leaking out of the urethra = extravasation, confirming the tear.

qs.q: Mention 2 options for initial management.
a: Suprapubic catheter (US-guided) for bladder drainage; endoscopic (primary) realignment with catheter placement.
qs.why: The bladder must be drained without crossing the injury (suprapubic catheter), or the urethra realigned endoscopically over a catheter.

title: Acute scrotum — testicular torsion
scenario: A male with acute severe left scrotal pain with nausea/vomiting, referred to the ipsilateral lower abdomen; prior episodes of self-limited scrotal pain and swelling. Photo shown. Archive

imgs.cap: Torsion — twisted spermatic cord with dark (infarcted) testis at exploration

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: Testicular torsion.
qs.why: Sudden severe scrotal pain with vomiting in a young male, with previous self-limited episodes (intermittent torsion) = testicular torsion.

qs.q: Mention three clinical signs.
a: Swollen tender red/dark scrotum, high-riding (horizontal-lie) testis, negative Prehn's sign (no relief on elevation), absent cremasteric reflex.
qs.why: The twisted cord shortens (high, horizontal testis), the cremasteric reflex is lost, and lifting the testis doesn't help (negative Prehn's).

qs.q: What are the 2 radiological investigations of choice?
a: Colour Doppler ultrasound; radionuclide scan (MRI for incomplete torsion) — but never delay surgery.
qs.why: Doppler shows absent blood flow — but torsion is a clinical diagnosis and imaging must not delay surgery.

qs.q: What is the treatment?
a: Urgent scrotal exploration, detorsion and bilateral orchidopexy (orchidectomy if non-viable).
qs.why: The testis dies within ~6 hours: urgent exploration and detorsion, fixing both testes because the bell-clapper anomaly is bilateral.

title: Digital rectal (prostate) examination
scenario: Prostate / DRE station (with the cystitis urinalysis station in the older files).

qs.q: How do you perform a DRE / prostate examination?
a: Consent, chaperone, left lateral position; inspect the perianal area; lubricated gloved finger: anal tone, rectal masses, prostate size, consistency (rubbery = BPH; hard/nodular = cancer; boggy/tender = prostatitis), median sulcus, symmetry, mobility of the rectal mucosa; inspect the glove (blood/stool).
qs.why: The posterior (peripheral) zone of the prostate — where cancers arise — lies against the rectum; consistency, nodules and loss of the median sulcus separate BPH, cancer and prostatitis.

title: Posterior urethral valves
scenario: A full-term 3.5 kg baby boy with bilateral hydronephrosis on antenatal US; cries when urinating, lower abdomen distended. Archive

imgs.cap: Voiding cystourethrogram — dilated, elongated posterior urethra; trabeculated bladder

qs.q: What is the name of this study?
a: Micturating (voiding) cystourethrogram — MCUG/VCUG.
qs.why: Contrast filling the bladder through a catheter with films during voiding = MCUG — the test that shows the posterior urethra.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Posterior urethral valves.
qs.why: A boy with bilateral hydronephrosis and a distended bladder with poor stream = posterior urethral valves.

qs.q: Describe 2 findings related to this abnormality.
a: Dilated, elongated posterior urethra with discrepancy between anterior and posterior urethra; thickened trabeculated bladder with hypertrophied bladder neck; vesico-ureteric reflux.
qs.why: The valve obstructs outflow, so the urethra above it dilates, the bladder thickens and trabeculates, and back-pressure causes reflux.

qs.q: What is the first line of management?
a: Bladder drainage (urethral catheter/feeding tube), prophylactic antibiotics, labs (electrolytes, creatinine, BUN), NICU support (pulmonary hypoplasia, renal insufficiency).
qs.why: Draining the bladder relieves obstruction immediately and allows stabilisation (NICU, creatinine after 48 h, antibiotics) before definitive surgery.

qs.q: What is the definitive treatment?
a: Cystoscopic (endoscopic) valve ablation; preterm/low weight/renal failure → cutaneous vesicostomy.
qs.why: Endoscopic ablation removes the obstructing membrane; vesicostomy diverts urine when the baby is too small for endoscopy.

qs.q: Identify the study and the diagnosis.
a: MCUG showing retrograde flow of contrast from the bladder into the ureter(s) ± dilated pelvicalyceal system → vesico-ureteric reflux (grade I–V).
Management by grade: continuous antibiotic prophylaxis & follow-up; endoscopic injection (Deflux) or ureteric reimplantation for high grade / breakthrough UTIs.
qs.why: On MCUG, contrast running up from the bladder into the ureters = VUR; its grade guides treatment (prophylaxis for most, surgery for high-grade or breakthrough infections).

title: Renal cell carcinoma
scenario: A 75-year-old man presented with flank pain; CT shown (in the old exam the mass was on the right side). Old exam

imgs.cap: Contrast CT abdomen — left renal mass (arrow)
Contrast CT — right RCC extending into the renal vein & IVC

qs.q: What is the modality of this investigation?
a: CT abdomen with IV contrast (mention the contrast — it is in the aorta).
qs.why: Contrast in the aorta shows it is a contrast-enhanced CT — needed to characterise renal masses.

qs.q: Mention the abnormality you see.
a: A mass in the kidney (mention the side).
qs.why: Describe a solid enhancing renal mass and its side.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Renal cell carcinoma (hypernephroma).
qs.why: A solid enhancing renal mass in an older adult = renal cell carcinoma.

qs.q: What symptoms may the patient present with?
a: Haematuria, flank pain, flank mass (classic triad), weight loss, HTN, anaemia (paraneoplastic); most often now an incidental finding on imaging.
qs.why: The classic triad (haematuria, flank pain, mass) is late; paraneoplastic features occur; most are found incidentally.

qs.q: What is your management if the lesion is localised?
a: Radical nephrectomy (partial nephrectomy for small tumours).
qs.why: Localised RCC is cured by surgery (radical nephrectomy, or partial for small tumours to save nephrons) — it is resistant to chemo- and radiotherapy.

title: Cystitis — urinalysis
scenario: Cystitis with urinalysis (the rest of the case wasn't recorded). Archive

qs.q: Interpret the urinalysis.
a: Pyuria (WBC too numerous to count), RBCs and bacteria; dipstick positive leukocyte esterase and nitrite; culture may be positive → bacterial cystitis (UTI).
qs.why: Leukocyte esterase (white cells) and nitrite (Gram-negative bacteria convert nitrate) with pyuria and bacteriuria = bacterial cystitis.

title: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
scenario: A 62-year-old man with difficulty initiating (or maintaining) micturition for 1 year, otherwise healthy. 439A

qs.q: Ask some questions in the history.
a: "FUN WISE": Frequency, Urgency, Nocturia, Weak stream, Intermittency, Straining, incomplete Emptying (+ haematuria, retention, UTI, weight loss/bone pain, drugs).
qs.why: LUTS are divided into storage and voiding symptoms; red flags (haematuria, weight loss, bone pain) suggest cancer.
hist: Storage symptoms from an irritable, unstable bladder.
Weak stream, intermittency, straining, incomplete emptying
Voiding symptoms from outflow obstruction by the enlarged prostate.
May be from prostatic vessels but cancer must be excluded.
A complication that needs urgent catheterisation.
Red flags for prostate cancer with bone metastases.
Anticholinergics and decongestants can precipitate retention.

qs.q: What investigations?
a: Urinalysis, CBC, RFT, PSA, US (prostate size, post-void residual) (+ DRE, uroflowmetry).
qs.why: Urinalysis excludes infection/haematuria, creatinine checks for back-pressure, PSA screens for cancer, US measures prostate size and residual urine.

qs.q: What is the management?
a: Medical: α-blocker (tamsulosin), 5-α-reductase inhibitor (finasteride).
Surgical: transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP).
qs.why: α-blockers relax prostatic smooth muscle (fast relief), 5ARIs shrink the gland (slow); TURP for complications or failed medical therapy.
